lines.trans: Vik, what is wrong?
What is the matter, Max?
What is the matter?
I almost got fired today.
And it is all thanks to you.
Max, you are ruining my life.
That is it.
I do not want to see you.
Want me to tell you what is going on?
You make everything so complicated.
Then you blame everyone else.
Maybe you should look at yourself for the reasons?

words.gloss: to look for, to search a bit

lines.trans: I have always wondered...
Why people build walls between themselves.
Kostya, how about we just sleep tonight too, okay?

lines.trans: But there are walls we build on purpose...
So we can enjoy tearing them down.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: in comparisons: больше, чем = more than

examples.text: А почему нет? Продавец получает больше, чем преподаватель.
examples.trans: Why not? A sales assistant earns more than a lecturer.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'matter', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('matter, business') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('case (in court)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'a little'.
чуть не + verb: я чуть не упал = I nearly fell

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'волить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to fire', forming an aspectual pair with 'увольнять'.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'work', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('job') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Russian preposition meaning 'thanks to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: And it is all thanks to you.
It is what earns us respect.

examples.text: Но благодаря вам у нас все получилось. Спасибо вам за вас.
examples.trans: But thanks to you, we made it work. Thank you for being you.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to ruin'.

examples.text: Не смей из-за одной глупой ссоры рушить нашу крепкую дружбу!
examples.trans: Do not dare ruin our strong friendship over one foolish quarrel!

examples.text: Опоздание поставщика может полностью рушить все наши планы на банкет.
examples.trans: A supplier's delay can completely wreck all our plans for the banquet.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to see', forming an aspectual pair with 'увидеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = see?') (drawing attention) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

examples.text: Ты видишь, сколько гостей сегодня вечером сидит в зале?
examples.trans: Do you see how many guests are sitting in the hall tonight?

meanings.note: once; что скажешь? = what do you say?
Secondary conversational sense ('tell me / tell us') (polite request) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'constantly'.

examples.trans: What are you constantly afraid of?
He was constantly late for work.
What are you constantly afraid of, Kostik?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'сложнять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to complicate'.
Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: short forms виноват / виновата / виноваты are used for 'it's my/your fault'

examples.text: Я ни в чём не виноват.
examples.trans: I'm not to blame for anything.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to make') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').
Secondary conversational sense ('different') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order
the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order

examples.text: То есть просто стоять и смотреть?
examples.trans: So we just stand and watch?

examples.text: Стоять на месте, никто не выходит из кухни без разрешения!
examples.trans: Freeze right there, nobody leaves the kitchen without permission!

поискать.gloss: to look for, to search a bit

meanings.en: to search for a while, to look around
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'искать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to look for', forming an aspectual pair with 'искать'.

examples.trans: I will look for another option.
You are right, I will look for another option.

examples.text: Может, стоит поискать причины в себе?
examples.trans: Maybe you should look at yourself for the reasons?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'чина'). Common feminine noun meaning 'reason, cause' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Нет причин держать вас под арестом.
examples.trans: There is no reason to keep you under arrest.

examples.text: Нет причин держать вас под арестом. Сегодня вы выйдете отсюда.
examples.trans: There is no reason to keep you under arrest. Today you will walk out of here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'дивлять'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to surprise', forming an aspectual pair with 'удивить'.

examples.text: Костик, ты снова удивляешь своей глупостью.
examples.trans: Kostik, you surprise me again with your foolishness.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: the plural is a different word: люди, людям, о людях
Secondary conversational sense ('people') (plural люди, a different word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'зводить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'erect, raise'.

examples.text: почему люди сами возводят между собой границы.
examples.trans: why people build walls between themselves.

examples.text: Но есть границы, которые мы специально возводим...
examples.trans: But there are walls we build on purpose...

meanings.note: meжду нами = between us; между прочим = by the way, for your information

examples.trans: For your information, I am the chairman of the court.
You two sort it out between yourselves here.

между.governs: instrumental (or genitive in a few set phrases)

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common feminine noun meaning 'border, boundary' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я улетаю за границу, поехали вместе!
examples.trans: I am flying abroad, let's go together!

meanings.note: давай + 1st person plural or infinitive
давай + 1st person plural or infinitive

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'too'.

examples.text: Мы же здесь выросли. И о людях тоже надо думать.
examples.trans: After all, we grew up here. And you have to think about people too.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: to take a rest or sleep temporarily

examples.trans: Let us just sleep quietly tonight.
All right, let us just sleep tonight.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: joins a description to a noun; agrees with that noun in gender and number

examples.trans: This is a mayor who keeps his word.
Where is the book that was here?

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: не специально = not on purpose, by accident
Secondary conversational sense ('specially, specifically') (for a particular purpose) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну перестаньте, вы же не специально!
examples.trans: Oh, stop it, you didn't do it on purpose!

examples.text: Я приготовил этот торт специально для вас.
examples.trans: I made this cake specially for you.
Are you doing this on purpose?

meanings.note: + past tense: 'чтобы свидетели были'
Secondary conversational sense ('in order to') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'довольствие'). Common neuter noun meaning 'pleasure' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Даже Лёша начал ходить в садик с удовольствием.
examples.trans: Even Lyosha started going to daycare with pleasure.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'рушить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to destroy', forming an aspectual pair with 'разрушать'.

examples.text: Ты разрушил мою семью своими фотографиями!
examples.trans: You destroyed my family with your photos!

examples.text: Ты разрушил такой прекрасный и сентиментальный момент!
examples.trans: You ruined such a wonderful and sentimental moment!
